## Learning Objectives

- Understand the **epidemiology** and evolving risk factors of HCC
- Describe the **molecular profile** of hepatocarcinogenesis
- Know current **screening strategies** and diagnostic criteria
- Master the **BCLC staging** system and prognostic evaluation
- Review **treatment approaches**: surgery, transplantation, ablation, intra-arterial and systemic therapies
- Explore **future prospects** in prevention and precision oncology

## Chapter Overview

- **Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)** is the most common primary liver tumor
- Results in approximately **800,000 deaths globally per year**
- Usually develops in the setting of **chronic liver disease**, particularly cirrhosis
- This chapter provides an overview of:
  - Epidemiology
  - Diagnosis
  - Therapeutic approaches

## What Is Hepatocellular Carcinoma?

- Most common **primary liver tumor**
- ~**800,000 deaths** globally per year
- Liver tumors worldwide:
  - **4th** leading cause of cancer death
  - **6th** most common neoplasia
- Usually arises on a background of **chronic liver disease**, particularly **cirrhosis**

## Global Burden of Disease

- Marked **geographic differences** in incidence
- **High-risk areas**: Asia and sub-Saharan Africa
  - Yearly incidence exceeding **20 cases per 100,000 population**
- Incidence rates and mortality are **increasing** in many parts of the world:
  - North America
  - Latin America
  - Central Europe
- Incidence appears to be **decreasing in Japan**

## Geographic Distribution by Etiology

- Varies widely according to **ethnic groups and regions**
- Clear association with exposure to:
  - **Hepatitis viruses**
  - **Environmental pathogens**
- **80% of cases** occur in:
  - Sub-Saharan Africa
  - West Asia

## Demographics

- Prevalence is **3-fold higher in males** compared with females
- Peak incidence around the **sixth and seventh decade** of life

## The Usual Setting: Chronic Liver Disease

- HCC usually develops in the setting of **chronic liver disease**
- Particularly in patients with **cirrhosis**
- Main background etiologies:
  - Chronic viral hepatitis **B (HBV)**
  - Chronic viral hepatitis **C (HCV)**
  - **Alcoholic** liver disease
  - **MAFLD** (metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease)

## A Reshaped Landscape of Risk Factors

The burden of risk factors and geographic distribution are being reshaped by:

- Implementation of **universal HBV vaccination**
- Widespread use of **direct-acting antivirals (DAAs)** against HCV
- Growing occurrence of **MAFLD-associated comorbidities**:
  - Obesity, diabetes, dyslipidemia
  - Frequently overlap with **excessive alcohol consumption**

## The Survival Gap

- HCC is a **major global health problem**
- Preventive and therapeutic strategies are areas of **increasing interest** among clinical researchers
- Nevertheless, the **5-year survival rate is between 5% and 15%**
- This reflects the **challenging management** of these patients

1. Epidemiology, risk factors, and prevention

## Section 1 · Epidemiology, Risk Factors, and Prevention

::: {.callout-note}
## Key question
What drives HCC risk, and how can it be prevented?
:::

- Cirrhosis as the major determinant
- Viral hepatitis (HBV, HCV)
- MAFLD and metabolic syndrome
- Prevention strategies

## Cirrhosis: The Major Determinant

- **Cirrhosis is the major determinant of HCC**
- Can be caused by:
  - Viral infections (**HBV and HCV**)
  - **MAFLD**
  - **Alcohol** intake
  - **Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency**
  - **Hereditary hemochromatosis**, among others

## Lifetime and Annual Risk in Cirrhosis

- **One-third** of cirrhosis patients will develop HCC throughout their lifetime
- **Annual risk of 1% to 8%**, depending on the etiology
- The risk is greater:
  - The more **relevant the signs** are
  - The more **severe the liver disease** is

## HBV: Geographic Patterns

- The majority of cases (**80%**) occur in:
  - **Sub-Saharan Africa**
  - **West Asia**
- These regions have:
  - High prevalence of **HBV infection**
  - Exposure to **aflatoxin B1**

## Aflatoxin B1 and p53

- Aflatoxin B1 is a **mycotoxin** produced by ***Aspergillus*** species
- Induces a **specific p53 mutation**
- This mutation offers **proliferation advantages** to hepatocytes
- Synergizes with HBV in high-risk regions

## HBV-Related HCC: Risk Factors

In addition to **cirrhosis**, the risk of developing HCC among patients with chronic HBV is related to:

- **High viral load**
- **Active viral replication**
- **Genotype C**
- Presence of **liver dysfunction**

## HBV: HCC Without Cirrhosis

- HBV-related HCC can develop **even in the absence of cirrhosis**
  - Occurs in **20% to 30%** of the cases
- **Inactive HBV carriers** are also at increased risk
  - Due to **HBV gene integration** into the host genome

## HBV Vaccination: A Prevention Success

- A significant impact on **reducing HCC-related deaths** through HBV vaccination has been reported
- Best documented in **endemic areas**, such as **Taiwan**
- Universal vaccination is reshaping the global burden of HCC

## HCV: Geographic Patterns

- In **Japan** and **Western countries** (especially Europe and the United States):
  - The main risk factor is **chronic HCV infection**
- HCC in patients with HCV occurs **almost exclusively** in the setting of:
  - **Advanced stage liver disease**
  - **Cirrhosis**

## HCV Treatment Reduces — But Does Not Eliminate — Risk

- Increasing evidence that **HCV treatment decreases** the risk of HCC
  - But **does not eliminate** it
- A meta-analysis: **sustained virologic response (SVR)** is associated with a **reduced risk** of developing HCC
- The rate of HCV-related HCC is expected to **decrease or stabilize** in the coming years

## The DAA Era

- **Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs)** are highly effective
- Induce **sustained virologic response** at higher rates compared with:
  - The ancient **interferon-based regimens**
- Expected consequence: decreasing/stabilizing HCV-related HCC incidence

## DAA Controversy in Previously Treated HCC

- It has been **hypothesized** that the use of DAAs in patients **previously treated for HCC** may be related to:
  - **Early recurrences**
  - **Aggressive biological behaviour**
- This raises concern about the wide applicability of DAAs in patients with past HCC
- **Still highly controversial**: major heterogeneity between studies prevents a robust conclusion

## MAFLD: An Emerging Epidemic

- A noticeable **transition in risk factors** has been observed in Western countries
- Growing evidence that **MAFLD** is an increasingly frequent liver condition in patients who develop HCC
- Often associated with other comorbidities:
  - **Obesity**
  - **Hypertension**
  - **Diabetes**
- Clearly **overlapping with alcohol consumption**

## MAFLD → HCC: Pathogenesis

- It is likely that MAFLD causes HCC **via cirrhosis**
- However, the **precise pathogenesis has not yet been elucidated**
- Some cases are reported to happen **in the absence of cirrhosis**

## Trends in Liver Transplant Etiology (US Registry, 2002–2016)

A national United States registry on liver transplantations between **2002 and 2016** showed:

| Etiology | Trend |
|---|---|
| HCV | Remained stable |
| Alcohol intake | Remained stable |
| HBV | Decreased |
| "NASH" (now grouped under **MAFLD**) | **Relevant increase** |

## Implications of the MAFLD Trend

- Projects an **ascending burden of MAFLD-related HCC** in the coming years
- Need to implement strategies to **prevent and reduce risk factors** associated with metabolic syndrome
- However, in patients with MAFLD the **main cause of death is cardiovascular events**
  - Stresses the need for a **multiorgan approach** beyond individual specialties

## Protective Factors

- **HBV vaccination**
- **Antiviral treatment** for both HBV and HCV
- Proper controls in **healthcare settings** prevent HCV dissemination through blood transmission

## Primary Prevention Measures

- **Alcohol intake** should be the target of health campaigns in the community
- **Aflatoxin** contamination of food can be prevented by:
  - Avoiding **grain storage in humid conditions**
- The epidemic of **obesity** must be controlled by **health education**

## Secondary Prevention

- Requires the **prior recognition of affected individuals** with chronic liver disease
- **No proof of cost-effectiveness** of population screening for liver disease has been offered

## Observational Protective Associations

Observational studies support that the following **reduce the risk of HCC**:

- **Statins**
- **Aspirin**
- **Coffee consumption**

::: {.callout-caution}
Additional evidence is needed to clarify if any alimentary or pharmacologic measure truly impacts in reducing the risk of HCC.
:::

## Risk Factors at a Glance

| Category | Factors |
|---|---|
| Viral | HBV (integration, genotype C, viral load), HCV |
| Environmental | Aflatoxin B1 |
| Metabolic | MAFLD, obesity, diabetes, dyslipidemia |
| Lifestyle | Alcohol |
| Genetic/other | Cirrhosis of any cause, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, hemochromatosis |
| Protective | HBV vaccination, antivirals, statins, aspirin, coffee |

## Section 2 · Molecular Profile

::: {.callout-note}
## Key question
Which molecular events drive hepatocarcinogenesis — and are they targetable?
:::

## Hepatocarcinogenesis: A Complex Process

- A **complex process** involving several:
  - Molecular landmarks
  - Signaling pathways
- Genomic analyses are **predominantly restricted to early-stage resected HCC samples**
- This inadvertently depicts early genetic and epigenetic events that might **not reflect intermediate and advanced stages**

## Most Frequent Molecular Alterations

- **Telomerase maintenance**
  - *TERT* promoter alterations
- **CTNNB1 / Wnt–Beta-catenin** pathway activation
- **p53** mutations
- **MAP kinase** signaling

## Targetable Pathways Under Exploration

Explored in translational research:

- Activation of **c-MET**
- **Fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR)**
- **Vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR)**
- **Transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β)**, among others

## Molecular Classification: Two Classes

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Proliferative class
- Activation of **RAS pathway**
- **FGF amplification**
- **HBV** infection
- **Poor prognosis**
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Nonproliferative class
- **Wnt–Beta-catenin** alterations
- **HCV** infection
:::
:::

## Whole-Genome Sequencing: Three Integrated Clusters

| Cluster | Features |
|---|---|
| **Cluster 1** | Low mutation frequency of *CTNNB1*; low expression of *TERT*; associated with **early stage** and **Asian origin** |
| **Cluster 2** | Higher prevalence of *TERT* promoter and *CTNNB1* mutations |
| **Cluster 3** | Higher prevalence of *TERT* promoter and *CTNNB1* mutations; **high p53 mutation occurrence** |

## Limitations of HCC Molecular Profiling

- Need to distinguish:
  - **"Driver" events** — fundamental for neoplastic transformation, with potential therapeutic applicability
  - **"Passenger" events**
- Genetic variations are **heterogeneous**:
  - Through **time**
  - Between **tumor sites** in the same individual
  - Even **within a single tumor site**

## Molecular Findings and Clinical Practice

::: {.callout-important}
In spite of the advances in molecular characterization of HCC, these findings have **not yet translated into substantial changes in the clinical setting**.
:::

## Section 3 · Screening Strategies

::: {.callout-note}
## Key question
Can early detection reduce HCC mortality — and who should be screened?
:::

## Purpose of Screening

- To **reduce mortality** through early detection
- Goal: detect HCC at a stage **amenable to curative treatment**
- Several uncontrolled studies suggest screening results in:
  - A higher proportion of **early diagnoses**
  - Higher **cure rates**
  - Better **prognosis**

## Landmark Evidence: The Chinese Randomized Trial

- More than **18,000 participants** with chronic HBV infection
- Randomized to screening with:
  - **Ultrasound + serum AFP every 6 months**
- HCC mortality was **significantly reduced** in the screening group:
  - **83.2 vs. 131.5** per 100,000 persons

## Caveats of the Evidence

- The trial had **low adherence** among participants
- Carried out in a population with a **particular risk factor (HBV)**
- Data have **not been reproduced globally**
- Reproducing such a trial seems **unfeasible for ethical reasons**
- Nevertheless, screening in patients with **cirrhosis** is widely established in clinical practice

## Selecting Individuals for Screening

Determined by:

- The **risk of developing HCC**
- **Life expectancy**
- Local **health structure conditions** that allow for proper treatment

::: {.callout-tip}
## Cost-effectiveness threshold
Screening should be applied when the risk of HCC is **at least 1.5% per year**, regardless of the etiology of liver disease.
:::

## Who Should Be Screened?

- **All patients with cirrhosis** who are potential candidates to receive anti-tumor treatment
- Some **subgroups without cirrhosis** with chronic HBV infection and high risk, according to recently proposed scores:
  - **PAGE-B**
  - **Toronto-THRI**
- Cirrhotic patients with **SVR after HCV treatment must remain under screening**
  - SVR does **not eliminate** the risk of HCC

## Unresolved Screening Questions

- **Noncirrhotic patients with HCV** (e.g., with bridging fibrosis):
  - It is **not clear** whether they should be screened
- **Nonviral etiologies such as MAFLD**:
  - It is **not defined** which subgroups benefit from screening
- Reasons:
  - **Heterogeneous incidence** of HCC within these scenarios
  - HCC can arise even **in the absence of cirrhosis**

## Screening Modality: Ultrasonography

- **Ultrasonography is the screening study of choice**
- Balances **cost and availability**
- Reported performance for screening liver tumors:
  - Sensitivity: **60% to 80%**
  - Specificity: **greater than 90%**

## Serum AFP: Strengths and Weaknesses

- Commonly applied in screening
- However, this marker has **low sensitivity**:
  - In general, **not increased in small tumors**
  - May be altered because of the **underlying liver disease**
  - Also altered in patients with **cholangiocarcinoma (CC)**
- Cirrhosis is also a **risk factor for CC**
  - A primary hepatic mass with increased AFP may correspond to **either HCC or CC**

## Emerging Biomarkers

Being analyzed for their role in early detection:

- **Des-γ-carboxyprothrombin (DCP)**
- **AFP-lectin**
- **Glypican-3**

## Screening Interval: Semiannual

- Recommended screening interval: **every 6 months**
- Based on estimates of **tumor growth rate**
- A prospective study showed:
  - **6-month interval** performed better than 12-month in detecting early lesions
  - **3-month interval** increased detection of small nodules **without impacting survival**
- The role of **CT and MRI** as screening for HCC is **not yet established**

## EASL and AASLD Recommendations

::: {.callout-tip}
## Guideline consensus
The **EASL** and the **AASLD** recommend **abdominal ultrasonography every 6 months**.
:::

- Because of the **suboptimal accuracy** of the AFP serum level:
  - Determination of this marker is **optional**

## Section 4 · Clinical Presentation

::: {.callout-note}
## Key question
How do patients with HCC present to the clinician?
:::

## Spectrum of Clinical Presentation

- A **range of clinical presentations**:
  - From **asymptomatic** (as in cases diagnosed in screening programs)
  - To **severe symptoms**
- Symptoms may occur because of:
  - The **underlying cirrhosis**
  - The **tumor growth and spread**

## Symptoms Due to Underlying Cirrhosis

- **Ascites**
- **Jaundice**
- Abdominal **collateral circulation**
- **Upper digestive hemorrhage**
- **Hepatic encephalopathy**

## Symptoms Due to Tumor Growth and Spread

- **Abdominal pain**
- **Weight loss**
- Palpable **abdominal mass**
- **Dyspnea**
- **Bone pain**

## Warning Signs

::: {.callout-warning}
## Red flag
A **sudden worsening of liver function** in a patient with otherwise stable chronic liver disease should be investigated for the possibility of HCC.
:::

- **Ascites** and **variceal bleeding** may develop because of:
  - **Portal vein** invasion
  - **Hepatic vein** invasion

## Paraneoplastic Syndromes

May be present and are generally associated with **poor prognosis**:

- **Diarrhea**
- **Hypoglycemia**
- **Erythrocytosis**
- **Hypercalcemia**

## Section 5 · Diagnosis

::: {.callout-note}
## Key question
How can HCC be diagnosed — often without biopsy?
:::

## Diagnosis in Cirrhosis: Imaging-Based

- For patients with **cirrhosis**, diagnosis can be made using **dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging**
- Based on the **neovascularization process** during hepatocarcinogenesis
- Key vascular difference:
  - **Malignant lesions** develop blood supply from the **hepatic artery**
  - **Nontumor liver parenchyma** supply is predominantly from the **portal system**

## The Radiologic Hallmark of HCC

- HCC nodules show:
  - **Contrast uptake in the arterial phase**
  - **"Wash-out" in the venous and late phases**
- Performance in liver nodules **larger than 2 cm** in the context of cirrhosis:
  - Sensitivity: around **80%**
  - Specificity: **at least 90%**

## Diagnostic Algorithm: Nodules < 1 cm

- On detection of an abnormal finding in ultrasonography, further evaluation must be performed
- Nodules measuring **less than 1 cm** in a cirrhotic liver:
  - May **not correspond to a malignant focus in greater than 60%** of cases
  - **Close follow-up in 3 to 4 months** is recommended

## Diagnostic Algorithm: Nodules > 1 cm

- In a cirrhotic liver, nodules **larger than 1 cm** can be diagnosed as HCC if:
  - The **vascular profile on imaging techniques is typical**
- In these cases, a **single dynamic imaging technique** can establish the diagnosis:
  - **CT** or **MRI**
- If the characteristic dynamic profile is **not recognized**:
  - **Fine-needle biopsy** is recommended

## Figure 89.1 — Typical CT Appearance of HCC

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
CT scan of a 3.5-cm nodule in segment VII, hypervascular in arterial phase and faint hypovascular in portal phase
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- CT scan depicts a **3.5-cm nodule in segment VII**
- **(A)** Hypervascular in the **arterial phase**
- **(B)** Faint hypovascular in the **portal phase** ("wash-out")
:::
:::

## Biopsy: Caveats

::: {.callout-caution}
It must be stressed that **biopsy is not 100% sensitive**; hence a **negative result does not exclude HCC**.
:::

## Tumor Markers and Immunohistochemistry

- Other tumor markers proposed (alone or in combination with AFP):
  - **Protein induced by vitamin K absence (PIVK)**
  - **AFP fractions**
  - **Glypican-3**
  - Their usefulness in routine clinical practice has **not been established**
- Immunohistochemical markers can increase the specificity of histologic diagnosis:
  - **Hsp-70**, **glypican-3**, **glutamine synthetase**
  - But they do **not replace expert pathology analysis**

## The Non-Cirrhotic Liver

::: {.callout-important}
In the context of a **noncirrhotic liver**, the diagnosis **must be made by histology**.
:::

- Imaging hallmarks validated in cirrhosis cannot be assumed in non-cirrhotic livers

## LI-RADS

- The **Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System**, proposed by the American College of Radiology
- Estimates the **likelihood of malignancy**
- Classifies lesions into **5 categories**:
  - From **definitely benign (1)**
  - To **definitely malignant (5)**
- Objective: provide guidance for subsequent management

## LI-RADS: Current Status

- May be useful for **homogeneous reporting**
- Seems to aggregate **little changes** to what is already current practice based on well-established radiologic criteria
- **Prospective studies** to define the role of LI-RADS in the clinical realm are **awaited**

## Section 6 · Staging and Prognostic Evaluation

::: {.callout-note}
## Key question
How do we integrate tumor burden, liver function, and patient status?
:::

## Dimensions of Prognostic Evaluation

Considering that the majority of patients with HCC have associated liver disease, prognostic evaluation should assess:

- The **extent of tumor involvement**
- The **severity of liver function impairment**
- **Performance status**
- **Cancer-related symptoms**

## Prognostic Systems: An Overview

A number of systems and algorithms have been proposed to predict prognosis for HCC:

- Cancer of the Liver Italian Program (**CLIP**) score
- Tumor-Node-Metastasis (**TNM**)
- Hong Kong Liver Cancer staging system
- Albumin-bilirubin (**ALBI**) score
- **Okuda** system

## Table 89.1 — Prognostic Systems in HCC (1/3)

::: {.smaller}
| Prognostic System (Year) | No. | Tumor Stage | Liver Function | Health Status | Stages |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Okuda (1985) | 850 | Tumor involvement > 50% | Bilirubin, albumin, ascites | — | I, II, III |
| CLIP (1998) | 435 | Tumor morphology, AFP, portal vein invasion | Child-Pugh | — | 0–6 |
| GRETCH (1999) | 761 | Portal vein invasion and AFP | Bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase | Karnofsky | A–C |
| AJCC TNM (2002) | — | Number of nodules, tumor size, portal vein invasion, metastases | — | — | I, II, III, IV |
| CUPI (2002) | 926 | TNM and AFP | Bilirubin, ascites, alkaline phosphatase | Symptoms | Score 0–12; 3 risk groups |
:::

| Prognostic System (Year) | No. | Tumor Stage | Liver Function | Health Status | Stages |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| SLiDe (2004) | 177 | TNM by LCSGJ | Liver damage by LCSGJ, PIVKA | — | 0–3 |
| Tokyo (2005) | 403 | Number of nodules and tumor size | Albumin, bilirubin | — | 0–8 |
| Taipei Integrated (2010) | 2030 | Total tumor volume and AFP | Child-Pugh | — | 0–6 |

::: {.smaller}
| Prognostic System (Year) | No. | Tumor Stage | Liver Function | Health Status | Stages |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **BCLC (1999)** | — | Number of nodules, tumor size, portal vein invasion, metastases | Child-Pugh, portal hypertension | PS | 0, A–D |

::: {.smaller}
*AFP = α-fetoprotein; BCLC = Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer; CLIP = Cancer of the Liver Italian Program; CUPI = Chinese University Prognostic Index; JIS = Japan Integrated Scoring; LCSGJ = Liver Cancer Study Group of Japan; PIVKA = protein induced by vitamin K absence or antagonist; PS = performance status; TNM = tumor-node-metastasis classification (AJCC/UICC).*
:::

## The BCLC Strategy

- The **Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC)** strategy has been widely validated
- Incorporates **all relevant dimensions** to predict prognosis:
  - **Tumor burden**
  - **Liver function**
  - **Cancer-related symptoms**
- Original version in **1999**; updated concepts incorporated over the years

## BCLC: Five Stages

The BCLC classification includes **five stages (0, A, B, C, and D)** according to prognostic variables related to:

- **Liver function** (preserved or end-stage liver disease)
- **Performance status** according to the ECOG scale
- **Tumor burden**

## Why BCLC Is Widely Accepted

- Links:
  - **Staging**
  - **Prognosis prediction**
  - **Clinical decision-making**
  - **Treatment indication**
- Has become a widely accepted clinical tool for treatment decision making (EASL, AASLD)
- The BCLC staging system **outperforms other prognosis systems**

## Figure 89.2 — BCLC Staging and Treatment Strategy

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
BCLC strategy: five stages linked to first-line treatment recommendations and expected median survival
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Establishes prognosis according to **5 stages** linked to **first-line treatment**
- Expected outcome expressed as **median survival** of each stage
- **Individualized decision-making** integrating the patient's medical profile
- Liver function evaluated **beyond Child-Pugh** (ALBI, MELD)
:::
:::

## BCLC Stage 0 — Very Early

- **Single tumor up to 2 cm**
- Absence of:
  - Vascular invasion
  - Cancer symptoms
- **Preserved liver function**
- Candidates for **curative local treatments**

## BCLC Stage A — Early

- **Single lesions irrespective of size**, or
- Up to **3 nodules of up to 3 cm**
- Absence of vascular invasion and cancer symptoms
- Preserved liver function
- Should be considered for **local treatments with curative intention**:
  - Surgical resection
  - Liver transplantation
  - Percutaneous ablation
- **5-year survival ranges from 50% to 70%**

## BCLC Stage B — Intermediate

- Patients with **multifocal tumors** and **preserved liver function**
- Should be considered for **TACE**:
  - May achieve a **50% survival rate at 3 years**
- Tumors should be **able to be selectively approached** to prevent damage to nontumoral liver
- Liver disease should be **compensated** (no clinically relevant ascites in need of treatment)
- **Diffuse, infiltrative, or extensive bilobar involvement** → consider **systemic therapies**

## BCLC Stage C — Advanced

- Patients with **preserved liver function** and one or more of:
  - **Extrahepatic dissemination**
  - **Vascular invasion**
  - Nonsevere impairment of functionality (**ECOG 1–2**)
- Benefit from **systemic treatment** with the aim to:
  - Increase survival
  - Improve quality of life
- Sequences of systemic agents provide an extended **overall survival of around 2 years**

## BCLC Stage D — Terminal

- Characterized by:
  - **Liver dysfunction**, or
  - Severe functional impairment (**ECOG 3–4**)
- **Dismal prognosis**
- Should receive **best supportive care** to minimize symptoms

## Section 7 · Treatment Approaches

::: {.callout-note}
## Key question
How do we match each patient to the optimal therapy?
:::

## Multidisciplinary Management

- Appropriate treatment selection is **complex**
- Patients with HCC should ideally be managed in **reference centers** with multidisciplinary teams including:
  - Hepatologists
  - Surgeons
  - Radiologists
  - Pathologists
  - Radiation oncologists
  - Clinical oncologists

## Levels of Evidence

- The level of evidence for many modalities is limited to:
  - **Cohort studies**
  - **Retrospective series**
- **Randomized studies** performed in the setting of **intermediate and advanced stages**
- Major research is needed in several scenarios

## The Treatment Arsenal

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
### Local
- Resection
- Transplantation
- Ablation
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
### Intra-arterial
- TACE
- TARE
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
### Systemic
- Tyrosine kinase inhibitors
- Monoclonal antibodies
- Immunotherapy
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
Guidelines and algorithms are useful for conceptualization and standardization, but the approach should be **personalized** according to each individual context.
:::

## Surgery: Liver Resection — Indications

- Treatment of choice for **localized HCC in the absence of cirrhosis**
- Patients with **compensated cirrhosis** should be thoroughly evaluated for the risk of decompensation
- In cases with **severe liver dysfunction**, surgery is **formally contraindicated**

## Assessment of Liver Function

- **Assessment of liver function is crucial** to achieving favorable outcomes
- Postoperative mortality is **significantly reduced** in patients with:
  - **Normal bilirubin**
  - **Absence of clinically significant portal hypertension**

## Assessing Portal Hypertension

- **Indirect markers**:
  - Thrombocytopenia
  - Esophageal varices
  - Ascites
  - Splenomegaly
- **Hepatic vein catheterization** is the most accurate tool:
  - **Hepatic pressure gradient < 10 mm Hg** is the best cutoff value
- Alternatively, **elastography** may establish clinically significant portal hypertension, avoiding catheterization

## Resection Outcomes

- In selected patients, **5-year survival rate reaches 70% to 80%** with surgical resection
- Patients with **portal hypertension** are at high risk for:
  - Liver decompensation
  - Death after surgery
  - Survival rates at 5 years of **50%**

## Tumor Selection for Resection

- Optimal results demonstrated in **single lesions**
- In some groups, selected cases with **two or three nodules** may be considered after careful evaluation
- **Tumor size is not a limiting factor**, but recurrence risk is higher the larger the tumor
- **Vascular invasion** denotes an elevated risk of systemic recurrence:
  - Ideally managed with **systemic therapy**
  - Some groups advocate resection for **segmental vascular invasion**

## Intraoperative Ultrasound

::: {.callout-important}
Despite advances in diagnostic capacity, **underestimation of tumour extension** continues to be a possibility.
:::

- **Intraoperative ultrasound** is essential to:
  - Detect potential unrecognized nodules between **0.5 and 1 cm**
  - **Optimize** the surgical resection efficacy
  - Instrumental to perform **anatomical resections**

## Figure 89.3 — Surgical Specimen of Segmental Resection

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Surgical specimen of a segmental hepatic resection
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- **Segment-oriented resections** maximize the elimination of **tumor satellites**
- This goal may be hampered by:
  - **Tumor size**
  - **Growth pattern**
:::
:::

## Minimally Invasive Liver Surgery

- **Laparoscopic-robotic surgery** allows a less invasive surgical treatment
- Provides **comparable results in terms of survival** with:
  - Lower perioperative **morbidity**
  - Shorter **hospital stays**
- No differences in operative time, blood loss, intraoperative complications, hospital stay, and morbidity between cirrhotic and noncirrhotic patients
- Laparoscopic approach appears to **reduce postoperative ascites, liver failure, and morbidity**
- May play a role in **"expanding indications"** beyond the "ideal candidate"

## International Consensus on Laparoscopic Liver Resection

Three international consensus conferences provided up-to-date summaries of status and perspectives:

| Year | Location |
|---|---|
| 2008 | Louisville, United States |
| 2014 | Morioka, Japan |
| 2017 | Southampton, UK |

## Predicting Recurrence After Resection

Disease recurrence might be predicted by pathologic findings:

- **Poor differentiation** degree
- Presence of **satellites / multifocality**
- Existence of **microvascular invasion**

::: {.callout-note}
## "Ab initio indication"
Because of the high risk of recurrence, at the BCLC it has been proposed to **enlist for transplantation** those patients with resected HCC who have pathology-registered pejorative histologic markers.
:::

## Adjuvant Therapy: An Unmet Need

::: {.callout-important}
There is **no proof of benefit** of any adjuvant therapy to prevent recurrence — and thus **no approach should be recommended**.
:::

## Liver Transplantation: Rationale

- Has the advantage of approaching **both**:
  - The **tumor**
  - The **underlying liver disease**
- Recommended as the **first-line option** for HCC within **Milan criteria**

## The Milan Criteria

- **1 nodule ≤ 5 cm**, or
- Up to **3 nodules ≤ 3 cm**
- In the **absence** of:
  - Portal invasion
  - Extrahepatic disease

Within Milan criteria:

- **5-year survival rate: 60% to 80%**
- **Recurrence rate: less than 15%**

## Beyond Milan

- The Milan criteria are widely used
- Increasing data suggest the potential benefit of liver transplantation in cases with **larger tumor burden**:
  - e.g., using the **UCSF expanded criteria**
- The level of **AFP** can also be used:
  - Levels **greater than 1000 ng/mL** are associated with **high risk of recurrence**

## Bridging Therapy

- Bridging therapies, such as **TACE or ablation**, are often needed for patients on the waiting list
- Purpose: **reduce the risk of tumor progression**
- Especially when the time on the list is **longer than 6 months**

## Downstaging

- **Locoregional therapies** can be used to increase eligibility for liver transplantation
- Key question: what criteria should be used for staging and potential downstaging?
- Results are **variable**, mainly because of differences in eligibility criteria:
  - Successful downstaging tends to be lower with more liberal criteria
  - Rates of downstaging achievement can reach **up to 90%** when more strict criteria are applied

## Living Donor Liver Transplantation

- Offers the possibility to **avoid waiting lists** for a deceased organ
  - Reduces the **dropout rate** and **time to transplant**
- Potential to provide access to transplantation for patients who otherwise would **not be eligible** for a deceased donor according to Milan criteria

::: {.callout-caution}
Living-donor transplantation must be **restricted to centers of excellence** to minimize donor risk and optimize recipient outcome.
:::

## Percutaneous Ablation: Techniques

- Proposed for patients with **liver-only disease** who are **not candidates for surgery or transplantation**
- Main techniques:
  - **Radiofrequency** ablation
  - **Microwave** ablation
- **Ethanol injection** can be used in particular situations:
  - Subcapsular location
  - In the vicinity of the gallbladder, blood vessels, or heart

## Ablation: Best Results

- Best results achieved in **solitary tumors smaller than 2 cm**
  - May achieve **complete necrosis**
  - Recurrence rates **comparable to resection**
- Tumors between **2 to 3 cm** or **up to three nodules** may also be treated percutaneously

## Ablation vs. Resection

- It has been suggested that **resection was not superior to ablation** in tumors of up to 3 cm
- There is a **need for further comparative trials** to validate these findings

## Radiotherapy in HCC

- **External radiotherapy** and **stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT)** have been explored in some settings:
  - e.g., **segmental portal vein invasion**
- **Encouraging results**
- Still **lacks robust evidence** on safety and efficacy

## Intra-arterial Therapy: Principles

- For patients with **liver-only HCC without vascular invasion** who are not amenable to resection, transplantation, or ablation
- Aim to **induce tumor necrosis**, exploiting the predominant **arterial blood supply** of HCC
- This allows for:
  - Selective infusion of **embolizing particles**, coupled or not with cytotoxic agents
  - Intraarterial infusion of **radioactive isotopes**

## TACE Techniques

- **Drug-eluting beads (DEB-TACE)** that slowly release chemotherapy
- **Conventional chemoembolization (cTACE)**:
  - Emulsion of cytotoxic agents with **lipiodol**, followed by **spongostan** injection
- The two seem to have **similar efficacy**
  - DEB-TACE is suggested to have **less toxicity and better tolerance**
- Both techniques are preferred over **bland embolization**, although there is no firm evidence of superiority

## TACE Efficacy

- Randomized trials and meta-analyses confirmed that **TACE improves survival** in cases not suitable for curative treatment
- Current expected **median survival** in patients selected according to evidence-based recommendations:
  - Around **30 months**
  - May even **exceed 40 months**

## TACE: Contraindications and Stage Migration

- **Absolute contraindications** to TACE:
  - **Decompensated cirrhosis**
  - **Severely reduced portal vein flow** (tumoral or nontumoral portal vein thrombosis)
- It is crucial to **assess liver function before and after every procedure** to prevent deterioration
- In the absence of objective response or untreatable progression:
  - **Systemic therapy** should be considered as part of a **stage migration strategy**

## TARE (Transarterial Radioembolization)

- Uses the injection of **⁹⁰Yttrium-labeled spheres** without the need for macroembolization
- No robust randomized studies comparing TARE with TACE
  - Data suggest **comparable tumor control rates**
- In patients with **BCLC C** stage:
  - TARE was **not superior to sorafenib**
  - Failed to enhance the benefit of sorafenib in **combination**
- More studies needed to place TARE into treatment algorithms and define subgroups that benefit

## Section 8 · Systemic Treatment

::: {.callout-note}
## Key question
From sorafenib to immuno-combinations — how far have we come?
:::

## Indications for Systemic Therapy

Recommended for patients with **preserved liver function** who:

- Present with **extrahepatic spread**, or
- Have **macrovascular invasion**, or
- Are **ineligible for liver-directed modalities** because of refractoriness or contraindication

## The Pre-2007 Era

- Until 2007, **limited therapies** existed for advanced stage disease
- Previous studies with **conventional chemotherapy** (e.g., doxorubicin and platinum combinations) resulted in:
  - **Significant toxicities**
  - **Modest efficacy**
- A resurgence of enthusiasm came with increasing knowledge on:
  - Molecular mechanisms
  - Intracellular signaling pathways
  - Angiogenesis

## Sorafenib: The Pioneer

- A **tyrosine kinase inhibitor** with antiangiogenic and antiproliferative activity
- The **first drug to demonstrate increased overall survival** in patients with advanced HCC
- Survival benefit was shown both in:
  - **Western** populations
  - **Asian** populations
- Pioneered the era of **systemic treatment in HCC**

## Regorafenib and the Concept of Sequencing

- **Regorafenib** has shown a significant increase in survival in patients with advanced HCC who had **progressed on sorafenib**
- An exploratory analysis showed that the sequence **sorafenib → regorafenib** provided:
  - A **median survival of 26 months**
- Reflects a significant advance in the treatment of advanced HCC

## Novel Targeted Agents

- **Lenvatinib** (tyrosine kinase inhibitor):
  - Proved **noninferior to sorafenib** in the first line
  - Approved as an **alternative to sorafenib**
- After progression to sorafenib:
  - **Regorafenib**
  - **Cabozantinib** (as second- or third-line)
  - **Ramucirumab** (in patients with **AFP of at least 400 ng/mL**)
- All based on positive results of **phase III trials**

## Immunotherapy: Rationale

The liver is a complex immunologic organ because of:

- Its **physiologic immunotolerance**
- The abundance of **immunosuppressive molecules** (such as **PD-1** and **PDL-1**)
- The fact that HCC develops mostly under **chronic inflammation** conditions

Immunity-modulating therapies are being studied in many active clinical trials.

## Immunotherapy: Early Results

- Preliminary results with **anti-PD1 antibodies** (nivolumab and pembrolizumab) showed:
  - **Encouraging response rates**
- However, they have **not compared favorably** with:
  - **Sorafenib** (in the first line)
  - **Placebo** (in the second line)

## Combination Breakthroughs

- **Atezolizumab** (anti-PDL1) + **bevacizumab** (anti-VEGF):
  - Improved survival in a **phase 3 trial in first-line** versus sorafenib
  - Included HCC patients with **very well preserved liver function**
- **Durvalumab** (anti-PDL1) + single dose of **tremelimumab** (anti-CTLA-4):
  - Improved survival over sorafenib
  - Durvalumab was **non-inferior** to sorafenib (randomized phase III trial)

## More Promising Combinations

Other combinations with encouraging results:

- **Nivolumab + ipilimumab**
- **Lenvatinib + pembrolizumab**

## Personalizing Systemic Therapy

Considering the increasing alternatives, the standard of care in advanced HCC is based on:

- **Selection of candidates**:
  - Performance status
  - Liver function
  - Degree of portal hypertension
  - Comorbidities
- Definition of the most suitable **sequence of drugs**
- Expected **incidence and severity of adverse events**

## Adverse Events: A Silver Lining?

- Interestingly, some adverse events are **associated with better outcomes**:
  - e.g., **dermatologic reaction** under sorafenib or regorafenib
- These should be seen **positively**
- Not as unnecessary **treatment interruptions**

## Section 9 · Future Prospects

::: {.callout-note}
## Key question
Where is the field heading — prevention, early detection, precision oncology?
:::

## Prevention Priorities

- **Prevention of HCC** in patients with chronic liver disease is essential
- Advances have been achieved with:
  - **Antiviral treatment**
  - **HBV vaccination**
- A trend toward increasing rates of **MAFLD-related HCC** underscores the need to broaden the preventive focus to causes of metabolic syndrome:
  - **Obesity**
  - **Diabetes**
  - **Dyslipidemia**

## Early Detection and the Recurrence Problem

- **Novel biomarkers and imaging tools** may allow detection of:
  - Dysplastic nodules **before malignant transformation**
  - Early-stage disease suitable for curative treatment
- Early diagnosis implies **better outcomes**
- But even after local treatment, the **probability of recurrence** is a matter of concern
- **Adjuvant treatments**, such as immune-oncology agents, are promising strategies to be tested
- **Close follow-up** is warranted — some local recurrences are still suitable for curative treatment

## Advanced Disease and Precision Medicine

- A significant proportion of patients are still diagnosed with **advanced stage**
- Many recurrences occur **outside the liver**
- **Systemic treatment** is probably the most evolving field in HCC:
  - From a context with **no effective drugs** in the early 2000s
  - To a situation with **several options**
- Active **translational research** should help develop **predictive biomarkers**:
  - Opening the doors to **personalized medicine and precision oncology**
  - Already in place in many neoplasms, but **not yet in primary liver cancer**

## Figure 89.4 — Interventions by Stage (Detail)

::: {.smaller}
| Stage | Preventive measures | Active treatment | Supportive measures | Areas of research |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Healthy liver | Primary: HBV vaccination, education, anti-alcohol campaigns, control of diabetes/obesity/dyslipidemia, testing high-risk groups, reduce aflatoxin | Diabetes, dyslipidemia, alcohol use disorders, obesity therapy | Primary care follow-up, governmental engagement | Prophylaxis (statins, aspirin, coffee), mass screening for viral hepatitis |
| Chronic disease / Cirrhosis | Secondary: semiannual screening, antiviral therapy, stop alcohol | Liver transplantation, antiviral therapy, control of metabolic risk factors | Specialist follow-up, screening for cirrhosis complications | Identify at-risk groups, screening methods, molecular risk scores, chemoprophylaxis |
| Liver-only HCC | Tertiary: post-treatment monitoring, screening for recurrence, management of adverse events | Local therapies, intra-arterial treatment, transplantation, systemic treatment | Multidisciplinary follow-up, symptom control, palliative care | Personalized therapies, predictive biomarkers, prevention of recurrence |
:::

## Key Takeaways (1/2)

- HCC is the **most common primary liver tumor**, causing ~**800,000 deaths/year**
- Usually develops on a background of **cirrhosis** (HBV, HCV, alcohol, MAFLD)
- The epidemiology is **shifting**: vaccination, DAAs, and rising MAFLD
- **Screening**: ultrasound every 6 months in at-risk patients (AFP optional)
- Diagnosis in cirrhosis can be made by **imaging** (arterial enhancement + wash-out)
- **BCLC** links staging, prognosis, and treatment — the most widely accepted system

## Key Takeaways (2/2)

- **Curative options**: resection, transplantation, ablation (5-year survival 50–80% in selected patients)
- **Intermediate stage**: TACE (median survival ~30–40 months with proper selection)
- **Advanced stage**: systemic therapy sequences — from **sorafenib** to **atezolizumab + bevacizumab** and **durvalumab + tremelimumab** (OS ~2 years)
- The future lies in **prevention, early detection, adjuvant strategies, and precision oncology**
